name: Monumbo
catalog_quote: Der Akzent ruht vorwiegend auf der vorletzten Silbe, namentlich im Plural, weniger häufig auf der drittletzten Silbe. In zusammengesetzten Formen wird der Akzent verschoben, so akú-atá = akunáta mein Vater, mér-kurún = mérkurun Knabe, kéatsak-kurún = keátkurun Mädchen.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (same penult penultimate stress; not in the strict set, i.e. OUT-strict / IN-dominant), unless the house strict-register definition explicitly tolerates an unlisted 'less frequently antepenultimate' minority
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim in the held archive.org PDF at printed p. 3 (PDF p. 17), end of 'I. Lautverhaeltnisse'; locator correct. (2) Deciding source: Vormann & Scharfenberger 1914, a 252-pp missionary reference grammar; it is the only grammar of the language (Glottolog full bibliography downloaded: everything later is wordlist/overview; Laycock 1975:776 'the only Monumbo-Lilau data extant', with the caveat 'unreliable on almost all other points' beyond noun classes and lexicon). the StressTyp2 entry for this language (penult, source = Vormann 1914) and Gordon 2002 derive from the same two sentences, so there is no independent second source. Best available: yes. sources.quote: "The accent rests predominantly on the penultimate syllable, especially in the plural, less frequently on the antepenultimate syllable. In compound forms the accent is shifted, e.g. akü-atá = akunáta 'my father', mir-kurún = mérkurun 'boy', kiatsak-kurún = keátkurun 'girl'." And p. 2: "In diphthongs the first element as a rule receives the stress."

sources.note: The only other first-hand linguistic treatment of Monumbo (Z'graggen 1969 calls it, with V&S 1914, the 'comprehensive' study; Glottolog types it wordlist, 44 pp). If it marks accent on its forms or comments on Vormann's Lautlehre it is the one place the 'vorwiegend penult / weniger haeufig antepenult' hedge could be tested, which decides strict vs dominant set for this record.
